## Introduction

In this task, you saw **10 words** presented one at a time and then tried to recall them in order.

The **Serial Position Effect** predicts that:

- **Primacy**: Words at the beginning are remembered better (more rehearsal time)
- **Recency**: Words at the end are remembered better (still in short-term memory)

::: {.key-finding}
#### Key Finding
On average, participants recalled **6.2 out of 10 words**, with clear primacy and recency effects visible in the data.
:::

## Load the Data

First, let's load our memory data. Run the code below:

## Overall Performance

How many words did participants recall on average?

```{webr-r}
# Summary statistics
memory |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_recalled = mean(total, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_recalled = sd(total, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_recalled = min(total, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_recalled = max(total, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

## Visualise Performance

Let's create a histogram of recall performance:

```{webr-r}
ggplot(memory, aes(x = total)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#27ae60", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(memory$total),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "#275882", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  labs(
    x = "Words Correctly Recalled",
    y = "Count",
    title = "Memory Performance Distribution",
    subtitle = "Blue dashed line = mean"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(color = "#275882", face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(color = "#275882")
  )
```

## Serial Position Effect

Now let's look at accuracy by position. The `pos` columns indicate:

- `1` = Correct position
- `2` = Recalled but wrong position
- `3` = Not recalled

```{webr-r}
# Reshape data to long format
position_data <- memory |>
  select(id, starts_with("pos")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("pos"),
    names_to = "position",
    values_to = "accuracy"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    position = as.numeric(str_extract(position, "\\d+")),
    correct = accuracy == 1
  )

# Calculate proportion correct at each position
serial_curve <- position_data |>
  group_by(position) |>
  summarise(
    prop_correct = mean(correct, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n()
  )

serial_curve
```

## Plot the Serial Position Curve

```{webr-r}
ggplot(serial_curve, aes(x = position, y = prop_correct)) +
  geom_line(color = "#27ae60", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(color = "#27ae60", size = 4) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.2, fill = "#27ae60") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 0.85, label = "Primacy Effect",
           color = "#275882", fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = 9, y = 0.85, label = "Recency Effect",
           color = "#275882", fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  labs(
    x = "Word Position",
    y = "Proportion Recalled in Correct Position",
    title = "Serial Position Effect",
    subtitle = "Do you see primacy (start) and recency (end) effects?"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(color = "#275882", face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(color = "#275882")
  )
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What Does This Show?

The **U-shaped curve** is a classic finding in memory research:

1. **Primacy** (first 2-3 words): High recall because you had time to rehearse them
2. **Middle**: Lower recall - too many words competing for attention
3. **Recency** (last 2-3 words): High recall because they're still in short-term memory

This supports the **multi-store model** of memory (Atkinson & Shiffrin, 1968).
:::

## Intrusions

Intrusions are words recalled that were **not** on the original list. Let's look at how many intrusions occurred:

```{webr-r}
ggplot(memory, aes(x = factor(intrusions))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#e74c3c") +
  labs(
    x = "Number of Intrusions",
    y = "Count",
    title = "Memory Intrusions",
    subtitle = "Words recalled that weren't on the list"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(color = "#275882", face = "bold")
  )
```

## Statistical Test

Is our recall significantly better than chance (guessing 1 out of 10 words)?

```{webr-r}
# One-sample t-test against chance (10% = 1 word)
t.test(memory$total, mu = 1)
```

**Interpretation**: If p < 0.05, we performed significantly better than chance!

---

::: {.key-finding}
#### Summary

The memory data shows clear evidence of the **serial position effect**, with better recall for words at the beginning (primacy) and end (recency) of the list. This supports classic memory theory.
:::
